Schools: every gym teaches one (Mexican, American, Cuban, Soviet, British, Filipino; in MMA, Dagestani, Brazilian jiu-jitsu, Dutch kickboxing, muay thai and collegiate wrestling). Mastery rises as you train and gives you advantages in fights.
  • Styles: acquired through affinity; at 60 you can switch, and at 70 in a second style you're a hybrid.
  • Blocks and fatigue: two-week blocks at light, normal or hard intensity; fatigue drops 20 a month and above 45 the injury risk rises.
  • Camp: before a fight, combine physical, technical and sparring blocks, and finish with a taper. Add special sessions such as video analysis of your opponent.
  • Amateur: every bout is recorded; with points or the national title you make the national team (stipend and international tournaments).
  • Purses: local and national shows pay according to each country's market; mandatory defenses can go to a purse bid (75/25).
  • Businesses: your own gym (members, coaches, fighters) and your own promotion (cards, tickets, television). They keep running after you retire, from the Career menu.

Coaches divide preparation into blocks of one to three weeks with one goal (strength, conditioning, technique, sparring) and taper before the fight. Training without rest leads to overtraining: lower performance and more injuries.

Each block raises several qualities at once and adds fatigue. Intensity changes the gains, the fatigue and the injury risk, which you see before doing it. If you have a scheduled fight, the blocks count toward your camp.
Accumulated fatigue is measured through training load, heart-rate variability and sleep. If you don't recover, overtraining and injuries appear.
It drops 20 points a month and a lot with "Active rest" or physiotherapy. Above 45 the injury risk rises and it reduces what you gain from training; above 70 you start the fight with less energy.

Professional teams hire specialists: video analysts, physiologists, nutritionists, sports psychologists and paid sparring partners. Altitude camps (like those in Big Bear, California, or in the State of Mexico) aim for more red blood cells.
Each session costs money and days, and has a cooldown. Video analysis reveals your opponent's exact attributes and adds technique if your plan is good against their style.
A typical camp lasts 6 to 12 weeks: physical base, technique, sparring tailored to the opponent's style and a taper with the weight cut at the end.
The score goes from 0 to 5: a physical block, a technical one, a sparring one, finishing with a taper (weight cut or rest) and 4 blocks or more. Each point adds energy at the start of the fight.

Every country develops its own way of fighting: the Mexican with pressure and body shots, the Cuban with defense and footwork, the Soviet with fundamentals and the jab; in MMA, Dagestani wrestling, Brazilian jiu-jitsu, Dutch kickboxing and muay thai.
Your gym teaches a school. Mastery (0–100) changes how much each attribute rises when you train and gives advantages in fights. Fighters around the world also have their country's school.
A style isn't fixed: many fighters change over the years or depending on the coach. The most complete ones combine two styles.

Affinity rises when you train what the style needs, with a school that teaches it and when you fight with its plan. At 60 you can adopt it (two months of adaptation); at 70 in a second style you're a hybrid.
Olympic amateur boxing is fought over 3 rounds with 10-point-must scoring. National federations keep rankings and form national teams that receive stipends and training camps.

Every bout is recorded. National ranking points come from your wins and medals and drop every year; with the national title or the top 2 you make the national team: a monthly stipend and access to international tournaments.
Specialized companies count the punches of every fight live (thrown, landed, power punches, jabs). In MMA they record significant strikes, takedowns and control time.
All your professional fights add up. On fight night you see them round by round with a bar chart and an attribute radar.
A boxing gym lives off its members' monthly fees; trainers of professional fighters usually charge around 10 % of the purses.
Members depend on reputation, the fee, the equipment and having coaches. You sign prospects who give you 10 % of their purses and who improve with the quality of your coaches.
Promotions pay the purses and collect tickets, TV rights, pay-per-view and sponsorships. Many local shows barely break even: the business is in developing fighters and in television.
Before every show you see the projection. Reputation rises with full venues, wins and titles, and unlocks the national and international levels and better TV deals.

When the champion and their mandatory challenger can't agree, the sanctioning body opens a bid among promoters: the highest offer wins and the purse is split according to the rules, often 70/30 or 75/25 in the champion's favor.
In this game the split is 75/25. The result of a purse bid can't be negotiated.
